questions.stem: According to collision theory, which two conditions must a collision between reactant particles meet to cause a reaction?
options: Enough energy to reach the activation energy, and a catalyst present
Enough energy to reach the activation energy, and a suitable orientation
Enough energy to reach the enthalpy change, and a suitable orientation
A suitable orientation, and particles of exactly equal masses
questions.explanation: A collision is successful only if the particles collide with at least the activation energy and in an orientation that lets the right bonds break and form. The enthalpy change is the overall energy difference, not the energy barrier, and many reactions proceed without a catalyst.

questions.stem: What is activation energy?
options: The average kinetic energy of the reactant particles
The minimum energy colliding particles need for a reaction to occur
The energy released when the bonds in the products of a reaction are formed
The difference in enthalpy between reactants and products
questions.explanation: Activation energy is the energy barrier: the minimum energy a collision must have to break bonds and start a reaction. The difference in enthalpy between reactants and products is ΔH, a separate quantity.

questions.stem: According to collision theory, why does increasing the concentration of a reactant in solution increase the reaction rate?
options: The activation energy of the reaction is lowered
The particles move faster because there are more of them
Particles collide more often, so successful collisions are more frequent
Each collision has more energy, so a larger fraction of collisions succeeds
questions.explanation: More particles in each unit of volume means more frequent collisions, so more successful collisions per second. The proportion of collisions with enough energy is unchanged, because that depends on temperature, not concentration.

questions.stem: In a reaction between two gases, the volume of the container is reduced at constant temperature. Why does the rate increase?
options: The pressure rises, so the particles have better orientation
The pressure rises, so the gas particles collide more frequently
The pressure rises, so each gas particle gains extra kinetic energy
The pressure rises, so the activation energy falls
questions.explanation: Squeezing the same number of gas particles into a smaller volume raises their concentration and pressure, so collisions are more frequent. At constant temperature the average kinetic energy of the particles does not change.

questions.stem: A 5 g lump of zinc and 5 g of zinc powder are each added to excess dilute sulfuric acid. Why does the powder react faster?
options: It lowers the activation energy because its bonds have been broken
It has a larger surface area, so more zinc atoms can be struck by acid particles
It has a smaller surface area, so the acid particles are concentrated on it
Its atoms have more kinetic energy because the particles are smaller
questions.explanation: Only zinc atoms at the surface can collide with hydrogen ions. Powdering exposes far more surface, so collisions are more frequent. Grinding does not change the activation energy or the temperature of the particles.

questions.stem: Increasing temperature increases both the frequency of collisions and the proportion of collisions with enough energy. Which statement about these effects is correct?
options: Neither effect matters, as temperature changes the rate by lowering the activation energy
The larger proportion of collisions with energy at or above Ea is the more important effect
The greater frequency of collisions is the only reason the rate rises at higher temperature
The greater frequency is more important, because energy does not affect whether collisions succeed
questions.explanation: A modest temperature rise increases collision frequency only slightly, but it substantially increases the fraction of particles with energy at or above the activation energy, which is the main reason the rate rises. Temperature does not change the activation energy itself.

questions.stem: Precipitation reactions between ions in solution, such as Ag⁺(aq) + Cl⁻(aq) → AgCl(s), are usually almost instant. What is the best explanation?
options: The reaction is catalysed by water molecules, which lower the enthalpy change
No existing bonds need to be broken, so the activation energy is very low
Many strong covalent bonds must be broken, so the activation energy is very high
Ions in solution have no kinetic energy, so they cannot move apart
questions.explanation: Oppositely charged ions attract each other and can combine without first breaking existing bonds, so the activation energy is very low and almost every collision succeeds. Reactions that must break strong bonds have high activation energies and tend to be slow.

questions.stem: Nitrogen gas, N₂, reacts very slowly with most substances at room temperature. Which explanation is best?
options: All of its reactions are endothermic, so they cannot occur at room temperature
Breaking its very strong triple bond gives reactions a high activation energy
Its weak single bond means reactions involving it have a low activation energy
Its molecules are too heavy to collide with other molecules often
questions.explanation: The N≡N triple bond is one of the strongest covalent bonds, so reactions that must break it have a large activation energy and few collisions at room temperature are energetic enough. Being endothermic does not stop a reaction from occurring, and nitrogen molecules are relatively light.

questions.stem: Which statement best describes how the bonds in the reactants are related to the rate of a reaction?
options: More and stronger bonds to break tend to give a higher Ea and a slower rate
More and stronger bonds to break tend to give a lower Ea and a faster rate
Stronger bonds in the reactants always make a reaction endothermic and fast
Bond strength sets ΔH only, so it has no link to the activation energy
questions.explanation: Activation energy reflects the energy needed to begin breaking bonds in the reactants, so reactions that require more or stronger bonds to be broken generally have a higher barrier, fewer successful collisions and a slower rate. Whether a reaction is endothermic depends on bonds formed as well as bonds broken.

questions.stem: What does a Maxwell-Boltzmann distribution curve show?
options: The enthalpy of the reactants and products along a reaction pathway
The rate of reaction at each temperature
The number of particles with each value of kinetic energy
The concentration of reactants at each point in time
questions.explanation: A Maxwell-Boltzmann curve plots the number or fraction of particles against kinetic energy. It shows that particles in a sample have a spread of energies, with only a small fraction having very high energies.

questions.stem: On a Maxwell-Boltzmann curve, how is the fraction of particles that can react shown?
options: By the area under the curve to the left of the activation energy
By the height of the peak of the curve
By the total area under the whole curve
By the area under the curve to the right of the activation energy
questions.explanation: Only particles with kinetic energy equal to or greater than the activation energy can react on collision, so the reacting fraction is the area under the curve beyond Ea. The total area represents all the particles in the sample.

questions.stem: When a gas sample is heated, how does its Maxwell-Boltzmann curve change?
options: The peak moves to higher energy and is lower, and the total area stays the same
The peak moves to higher energy and is taller, and the total area increases
The peak moves to lower energy and is taller, and the total area stays the same
The curve keeps its shape, but the activation energy line moves to the left
questions.explanation: At higher temperature the particles have a higher average kinetic energy, so the curve flattens and shifts right. The number of particles is unchanged, so the area under the curve stays the same. Heating does not move the activation energy.

questions.stem: How does adding a catalyst appear on a Maxwell-Boltzmann distribution for a reaction mixture at constant temperature?
options: The curve becomes taller and narrower, so fewer particles have low energies
The curve is unchanged, and the activation energy line moves to a higher energy
The curve is unchanged, but a lower activation energy line has more area beyond it
The curve shifts to the right, so more particles pass the same activation energy
questions.explanation: A catalyst does not change the energies of the particles, so the distribution stays the same. It provides a pathway with a lower activation energy, so the line marking Ea moves left and a larger area lies beyond it. Shifting the curve to the right is what a temperature rise does.

questions.stem: How does a catalyst increase the rate of a reaction?
options: It makes the reaction more exothermic by lowering the products' enthalpy
It increases the concentration of the reactants
It provides an alternative pathway with a lower activation energy
It gives the reactant particles more kinetic energy
questions.explanation: A catalyst offers a different reaction pathway whose energy barrier is lower, so a greater fraction of collisions succeed at the same temperature. It does not change the energies of the reactants or products, so ΔH stays the same.

questions.stem: What happens to a catalyst during a reaction it speeds up?
options: It is chemically unchanged at the end of the reaction
It is used up and must be added continuously to the mixture
It becomes one of the products of the reaction
It is converted into the reactants
questions.explanation: A catalyst may take part in intermediate steps, but it is regenerated, so it is chemically unchanged at the end. This is why only small amounts are needed.

questions.stem: On an energy profile diagram, the reactants are at 50 kJ mol⁻¹, the peak is at 180 kJ mol⁻¹ and the products are at 20 kJ mol⁻¹. What are the activation energy and ΔH?
options: Ea = 180 kJ mol⁻¹, ΔH = −30 kJ mol⁻¹
Ea = 130 kJ mol⁻¹, ΔH = +30 kJ mol⁻¹
Ea = 160 kJ mol⁻¹, ΔH = −30 kJ mol⁻¹
Ea = 130 kJ mol⁻¹, ΔH = −30 kJ mol⁻¹
questions.explanation: Ea is measured from the reactants up to the peak: 180 − 50 = 130 kJ mol⁻¹. ΔH = H(products) − H(reactants) = 20 − 50 = −30 kJ mol⁻¹, so the reaction is exothermic. The value 160 is measured from the products, which is the activation energy of the reverse reaction.

questions.stem: For the reaction in an energy profile with reactants at 50 kJ mol⁻¹ and products at 20 kJ mol⁻¹, a catalyst lowers the peak from 180 to 120 kJ mol⁻¹. What are the catalysed Ea and ΔH?
options: Ea = 70 kJ mol⁻¹, ΔH = −90 kJ mol⁻¹
Ea = 120 kJ mol⁻¹, ΔH = −30 kJ mol⁻¹
Ea = 100 kJ mol⁻¹, ΔH = +30 kJ mol⁻¹
Ea = 70 kJ mol⁻¹, ΔH = −30 kJ mol⁻¹
questions.explanation: The catalysed Ea is 120 − 50 = 70 kJ mol⁻¹. The energies of the reactants and products are unchanged, so ΔH is still 20 − 50 = −30 kJ mol⁻¹. A catalyst lowers the barrier, not the overall enthalpy change.

questions.stem: On an energy profile diagram for an endothermic reaction, which statement is true?
options: The products are higher than the reactants, and Ea is less than ΔH
The products and reactants are level, and Ea equals zero
The products are higher than the reactants, and Ea is greater than ΔH
The products are lower than the reactants, and Ea is greater than ΔH
questions.explanation: In an endothermic reaction the products have more enthalpy than the reactants, so ΔH is positive. The peak must lie above the products, so the activation energy is always larger than ΔH for an endothermic reaction.

questions.stem: A reaction has a forward activation energy of 90 kJ mol⁻¹ and ΔH = −40 kJ mol⁻¹. What is the activation energy of the reverse reaction?
options: 130 kJ mol⁻¹
50 kJ mol⁻¹
90 kJ mol⁻¹
40 kJ mol⁻¹
questions.explanation: The products lie 40 kJ mol⁻¹ below the reactants, and the peak lies 90 kJ mol⁻¹ above the reactants, so from the products the climb to the peak is 90 + 40 = 130 kJ mol⁻¹. Subtracting gives 50, which would place the products above the reactants.

questions.stem: Catalase, an enzyme, speeds up the decomposition of hydrogen peroxide in cells. Which statement about catalase is correct?
options: It lowers the activation energy and is not used up in the reaction
It raises the temperature of the cell so that more collisions succeed
It makes the decomposition more exothermic, releasing more energy
It reacts with hydrogen peroxide to form a new permanent product
questions.explanation: Enzymes are biological catalysts: they provide a pathway with a lower activation energy and are regenerated at the end of each reaction. They do not change the enthalpy change of the reaction or heat the cell.

questions.stem: Which change would decrease the rate of the reaction between marble chips and hydrochloric acid?
options: Crushing the marble chips into powder
Warming the acid before adding it
Using more concentrated acid
Using more dilute acid
questions.explanation: More dilute acid has fewer hydrogen ions per unit volume, so collisions with the marble surface are less frequent. Crushing, warming and concentrating the acid all increase the rate.

questions.stem: Food is kept in a refrigerator to slow spoilage. Which explanation in terms of collision theory is correct?
options: The concentration of the reactants in the food is reduced by the cold
The cold acts as a catalyst for reactions that preserve the food
Fewer particles have enough energy to overcome the activation energy
The activation energy of the spoilage reactions is raised by the cold
questions.explanation: At lower temperature, fewer particles have kinetic energy at or above the activation energy, and collisions are slightly less frequent, so spoilage reactions slow down. The activation energy itself is a property of the reaction pathway and is not raised by cooling.

questions.stem: Fine flour dust suspended in air can explode, while a heap of flour burns only slowly. Which factor explains this?
options: The higher concentration of oxygen in the heap
The lower activation energy of flour in a heap
The lower temperature of the suspended dust
The very large surface area of the dust
questions.explanation: Each tiny dust particle is surrounded by air, so the surface area in contact with oxygen is enormous and combustion happens extremely fast. In a heap, only the surface is exposed to oxygen. Dispersing the flour does not change the activation energy.

questions.stem: Which factor changes the reaction rate only for reactions involving gases?
options: Surface area
Pressure
Temperature
Catalyst
questions.explanation: Changing pressure alters the concentration of gas particles, but has almost no effect on the concentration of solids or liquids. Temperature and catalysts affect all reactions, and surface area matters for reactions involving a solid.

questions.stem: Which pair of changes would both increase the rate of reaction between magnesium ribbon and hydrochloric acid?
options: Warming the acid and using more concentrated acid
Cooling the acid and using more concentrated acid
Warming the acid and using more dilute acid
Using larger pieces of magnesium and cooler acid
questions.explanation: Warmer acid gives more collisions with energy at or above Ea, and more concentrated acid gives more frequent collisions, so both raise the rate. Cooling, diluting and using larger pieces with less surface area all slow the reaction.

questions.stem: A student adds 0.50 g of manganese(IV) oxide to hydrogen peroxide solution, which then decomposes rapidly. Afterwards the solid is filtered, washed and dried. What mass is expected?
options: 0.50 g, because a catalyst is not used up
Less than 0.50 g, because the catalyst was consumed
More than 0.50 g, because oxygen was added to it
0 g, because the catalyst dissolved in the solution
questions.explanation: Manganese(IV) oxide acts as a catalyst for the decomposition of hydrogen peroxide into water and oxygen. A catalyst is regenerated, so the same mass is recovered. If it were consumed it would be a reactant, not a catalyst.

questions.stem: In a reaction, the concentration of a product rises from 0 to 0.060 mol L⁻¹ in 30 s. What is the average rate of formation of the product?
options: 500 mol L⁻¹ s⁻¹
0.0200 mol L⁻¹ s⁻¹
0.0020 mol L⁻¹ s⁻¹
1.8 mol L⁻¹ s⁻¹
questions.explanation: Rate = Δ[P] ÷ time = 0.060 ÷ 30 = 0.0020 mol L⁻¹ s⁻¹. Multiplying the concentration by the time gives 1.8, and dividing time by concentration gives 500, neither of which has units of concentration per time.

questions.stem: The concentration of a reactant falls from 0.80 mol L⁻¹ to 0.50 mol L⁻¹ over 2.0 minutes. What is the average rate of the reaction in mol L⁻¹ s⁻¹?
questions.explanation: Rate = −Δ[R] ÷ time = (0.80 − 0.50) ÷ 120 s = 0.0025 mol L⁻¹ s⁻¹. The value 0.15 is the rate per minute, and 0.0042 uses the final concentration of 0.50 instead of the change.

questions.stem: Hydrochloric acid reacts with marble chips, and 45 mL of carbon dioxide is collected in the first 15 s. What is the average rate of gas production over this time?
options: 0.33 mL s⁻¹
675 mL s⁻¹
30 mL s⁻¹
3.0 mL s⁻¹
questions.explanation: Average rate = volume of gas ÷ time = 45 ÷ 15 = 3.0 mL s⁻¹. Dividing the time by the volume gives 0.33, which has the wrong units.

questions.stem: Marble chips react with acid in an open flask on a balance. The mass falls from 152.40 g to 151.52 g in 40 s as CO₂ escapes. What is the average rate of CO₂ production in mol s⁻¹?
questions.explanation: Mass of CO₂ lost = 152.40 − 151.52 = 0.88 g, so n = 0.88 ÷ 44.01 = 0.0200 mol, and rate = 0.0200 ÷ 40 = 5.0 × 10⁻⁴ mol s⁻¹. The value 2.2 × 10⁻² is the rate in grams per second, and 2.0 × 10⁻² is the total amount, not a rate.

questions.stem: On a graph of volume of gas produced against time, how is the rate of reaction at a particular instant found?
options: From the area under the curve up to that time
From the total volume divided by the total reaction time
From the gradient of the tangent to the curve at that time
From the volume of gas read off the curve at that time
questions.explanation: The instantaneous rate is the gradient of the curve at that point, found by drawing a tangent and calculating rise over run. Total volume divided by total time gives an average rate over the whole reaction, not the rate at one instant.

questions.stem: A tangent drawn to a gas volume-time curve at t = 20 s passes through (0 s, 10 mL) and (40 s, 50 mL). What is the rate at t = 20 s?
options: 1.25 mL s⁻¹
2.5 mL s⁻¹
1.0 mL s⁻¹
1.5 mL s⁻¹
questions.explanation: Gradient = (50 − 10) ÷ (40 − 0) = 40 ÷ 40 = 1.0 mL s⁻¹. Using 50 ÷ 40 gives 1.25, which ignores that the tangent does not start at zero volume.

questions.stem: On a graph of product volume against time, the curve is steepest at the start and becomes horizontal later. Why does it level off?
options: The temperature has risen, which stops the reaction
A limiting reactant has been used up, so no more product forms
The catalyst has been used up, so the reaction has stopped
The activation energy has risen as the product accumulated
questions.explanation: The rate falls as reactants are used up and their concentration drops, and the curve becomes horizontal once the limiting reactant is gone. A catalyst is not consumed, and activation energy does not rise during a reaction.

questions.stem: Trial A: 1.0 g of calcium carbonate chips with excess 1.0 mol L⁻¹ HCl at 20 °C. Trial B: identical but at 40 °C. How does the volume-time curve for B compare with A?
options: Steeper at the start, levelling off at twice the final volume
Less steep at the start, levelling off at the same final volume
The same initial gradient, levelling off at a higher final volume
Steeper at the start, levelling off at the same final volume
questions.explanation: At the higher temperature a larger fraction of collisions are successful, so B starts faster. The mass of calcium carbonate, the limiting reactant, is the same, so the same total volume of CO₂ is produced.

questions.stem: Trial A uses 2.0 g of magnesium ribbon with excess acid. Trial B uses 1.0 g of magnesium powder with the same volume and concentration of acid. Which description of B's hydrogen volume-time curve is correct?
options: Less steep at first, levelling off at twice the final volume of A
Steeper at first, levelling off at half the final volume of A
Steeper at first, levelling off at the same final volume as A
Less steep at first, levelling off at half the final volume of A
questions.explanation: The powder has a larger surface area, so B reacts faster at first. Magnesium is the limiting reactant, and B has half as much, so it produces half the volume of hydrogen. Surface area changes the rate, not the amount of product.

questions.stem: Which statement correctly distinguishes average rate from instantaneous rate?
options: Average rate is measured with a catalyst; instantaneous rate is measured without one
Average rate is the change over a time interval; instantaneous rate is the gradient at one moment
Average rate is the gradient at one moment; instantaneous rate is the change over a time interval
Average rate applies only to reactants; instantaneous rate applies only to products
questions.explanation: An average rate is the total change in amount or concentration divided by the time interval. An instantaneous rate is the gradient of the tangent at a particular time, and for most reactions it is greatest at the start.

questions.stem: For a reaction, a graph of reactant concentration against time is a downward curve. Which statement about the graph is correct?
options: The gradient is constant, because the activation energy does not change
The gradient is positive, because the rate of a reaction is always a positive number
The gradient becomes less steep over time, because the rate falls as reactant is used
The gradient becomes steeper over time, because product builds up and speeds the reaction
questions.explanation: As the reactant is consumed, its concentration falls, collisions become less frequent and the rate decreases, so the curve flattens. The gradient of a reactant concentration graph is negative; the rate is reported as a positive value by using −Δ[R] ÷ time.

questions.stem: A student measures the time for a cross under a flask to disappear as sodium thiosulfate reacts with acid. How is the rate related to the time taken?
options: The rate is proportional to 1 ÷ time
The rate is proportional to the time
The rate is equal to the time squared
The rate is proportional to √time
questions.explanation: A fixed amount of sulfur precipitate must form to hide the cross, so a shorter time means a faster reaction. The rate is therefore proportional to the reciprocal of the time.
